title: The Eve of St Agnes: date and occasion
short: Written at Chichester and Bedhampton in January-February 1819 and revised that September, the poem was published in Keats's 1820 volume.
body: Keats began the poem in January 1819 while staying at Chichester (probably about the feast itself), finished a draft at Bedhampton by early February, and revised it at Winchester in September 1819. It appeared in Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems (1820), the text printed here. The poem opens on 20 January, the eve of the feast of St Agnes (21 January), with an exclamation of pure sensation: before any story begins, the reader is made to feel the cold. It is often supposed, though this is an inference rather than a documented fact, that Isabella Jones, a friend of Keats, suggested the St Agnes subject. The frame of extreme cold, set against the warmth and colour of Madeline's chamber, structures the whole work.

anchor: The owl, for all his feathers
title: Spenserian stanza
short: The poem's 42 stanzas use Spenser's form: eight pentameter lines and a closing alexandrine, rhymed ababbcbcc.
body: Keats borrows the nine-line stanza of The Faerie Queene: eight iambic pentameters followed by a six-stress alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc. The interlocking rhymes slow narrative motion and favour description, which suits a poem of tableaux; the long last line often closes a stanza with a lingering image ('Past the sweet Virgin's picture, while his prayer he saith'). Keats had begun his career imitating Spenser, and the form also links the poem to its Romantic revivals (Thomson, Beattie, Byron's Childe Harold). Note how the alexandrines carry the poem's key turns, such as the rose that shuts 'and be a bud again' (st. 27).

title: Beadsman
short: A beadsman is a pensioner paid or housed to pray for the souls of a patron and his family; 'told' his rosary means counted its beads.
body: A 'bead' was originally a prayer (Old English gebed); a beadsman was one who prayed for another, often an almsman maintained by a great family to say prayers for its dead. 'Told' (l. 5) is the old sense of 'counted', as in a teller of votes. The aged Beadsman frames the whole poem: he opens it, passes the frozen effigies of the 'sculptur'd dead', and closes it, dead 'among his ashes cold' after 'thousand aves told'. Critics read him as the poem's figure of ascetic denial, the opposite of the lovers' sensual warmth, and his breath 'taking flight for heaven, without a death' anticipates the poem's play on dying and transport.

title: purgatorial rails
short: The iron railings round the tomb-effigies suggest to the Beadsman the bars of Purgatory, where the dead suffer before release.
body: The chapel tombs carry carved knights and ladies 'praying in dumb orat'ries' (small chapels or prayer-niches). Fenced by black iron rails, they appear imprisoned, and the Beadsman's imagination, steeped in Catholic doctrine, pictures them aching in 'icy hoods and mails' (mail armour) in Purgatory. The stanza projects the cold of the night onto the dead and shows the Beadsman's sympathetic, morbid piety. The medieval Catholic setting is a romance convention rather than a historical reconstruction. The frozen statues contrast with the 'carved angels, ever eager-eyed' of the banqueting hall (st. 4), and with Porphyro later 'pale as smooth-sculptured stone' (st. 34).

title: argent revelry
short: 'Argent' is heraldic silver: the guests burst in glittering in silver finery, the first of many heraldic colour words in the poem.
body: 'Argent' is the heraldic term for silver (Latin argentum). The phrase transfers the glitter of the guests' costumes to their revelry itself. Keats then distances the reader from the crowd: they are 'Numerous as shadows haunting fairily / The brain, new stuff'd, in youth, with triumphs gay / Of old romance', a self-conscious admission that this castle is made of literary memories. 'These let us wish away', the narrator says, turning 'sole-thoughted' to Madeline. Heraldic vocabulary returns in the casement's 'heraldries' and 'scutcheon' and in the 'gules' thrown on Madeline (st. 24-25).

title: The St Agnes' Eve rite
greek: Greek hagne, pure; Latin agnus, lamb
short: Folk belief held that a girl who fasted and went to bed in silence on St Agnes' Eve, looking neither behind nor sideways, would dream of her future husband.
body: St Agnes, a girl martyred at Rome c. 304, was patron of virgins; her name was linked both to Greek hagne (chaste) and Latin agnus (lamb), hence her emblem. Popular custom made the eve of her feast (21 January) a night of divination: a maiden going supperless to bed and lying on her back, without looking behind her, would see her future lover in a dream. Keats would have found the superstition in Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, his favourite book in 1819, which mentions fasting on St Agnes' Eve to learn one's future husband, and it was also known from Ben Jonson. Keats turns the rite into the poem's machine: Madeline's obedience to it makes her vulnerable to Porphyro's 'stratagem'.

title: Hoodwink'd: seduction or ascent?
short: The word 'hoodwink'd' (blindfolded, deceived) gives its name to the main critical debate over whether Madeline is spiritually exalted or simply duped.
body: To 'hoodwink' was literally to blindfold with a hood, hence to deceive. Madeline is blinded by 'faery fancy', and the poem's language of deception (stratagem, 'peeping', 'traitor', 'deceived thing') supports a sceptical reading. Earl Wasserman (1953) read the poem as a metaphysical allegory in which the lovers ascend through dream to a spiritual reality, Porphyro's progress mirroring the soul's approach to heaven. Jack Stillinger's influential 'The Hoodwinking of Madeline' (1961) replied that Porphyro is closer to a predatory seducer, a 'peeping Tom', and that Madeline is a self-deceived dreamer whom the poem gently mocks. Most later critics hold both readings in tension: the romance is lovely and also knowingly ironic.

title: amort
greek: French a la mort, to the death
short: 'Amort' means lifeless or dead to everything: Madeline is insensible to all around her except St Agnes and her dream.
body: 'All amort' is an Elizabethan phrase, from French a la mort, meaning spiritless or as if dead; Shakespeare uses it in The Taming of the Shrew (4.3, 'What, sweeting, all amort?'). Madeline, dancing 'with vague, regardless eyes', is dead to the timbrels and the 'throng'd resort' of whisperers, and alive only to St Agnes and the promised bliss. The archaism is typical of the poem's pseudo-medieval diction, which Keats drew partly from Spenser, Chatterton and Shakespeare.

title: St Agnes's lambs and the holy loom
short: On St Agnes's feast two lambs are blessed in her Roman church; their wool is later spun and woven by nuns into the pallium worn by archbishops.
body: The custom, which Keats knew at least in outline, is still observed: on 21 January two lambs are blessed at the basilica of Sant'Agnese in Rome, and their wool is woven by religious sisters into pallia, the woollen bands given by the Pope to archbishops. Hence Porphyro's oath 'by the holy loom / Which none but secret sisterhood may see, / When they St. Agnes' wool are weaving piously' (st. 13). The 'lambs unshorn' are thus the lambs not yet sheared for that wool. The image ties Madeline's virginity to sacrificial innocence: Agnes is the virgin martyr whose emblem is the lamb.

title: Porphyro
short: The hero's invented name evokes purple (Greek porphyra), the colour of royalty, passion and blood, and the 'purple riot' of his desire (st. 16).
body: Keats coined the name. It derives from Greek porphyra, the purple dye, and suggests porphyry, a purplish stone, and the Byzantine 'porphyrogenitus', one born in the purple. Critics connect it with the 'purple riot' of his thought in stanza 16 and with the poem's crimson and gules. Porphyro is from a hostile family, and the feud ('barbarian hordes, / Hyena foemen') recalls Romeo among the Capulets; Keats had been reading Shakespeare closely. His 'heart on fire' sets him against the poem's cold from the start.

title: beldame; Angela
short: 'Beldame' (literally 'fair lady') had come to mean an old woman, often a hag; Angela plays the part of Juliet's Nurse.
body: 'Beldame' began as a respectful term for a grandmother (French belle dame) and declined into 'old woman, crone'. The word also anticipates, ironically, the 'belle dame sans mercy' of stanza 33. Angela, the aged servant who calls Porphyro 'child' and is called 'Gossip' (a godmother or familiar old friend), recalls the Nurse in Romeo and Juliet, the go-between who helps the lovers against her own family. She is the poem's moral alarm ('A cruel man and impious thou art'), but is persuaded. Her death 'palsy-twitch'd' in the final stanza is among the details that darken the ending.

title: Merlin's monstrous debt
short: An obscure line usually taken to allude to Merlin's demonic parentage and his entrapment by the enchantress Vivien (Nimue); readings differ.
body: In Arthurian legend Merlin was begotten by a demon (an incubus) on a mortal woman; late in life he was beguiled by the enchantress Nimue or Vivien, who used the magic he had taught her to imprison him for ever. Some editors take the 'monstrous debt' to be Merlin's life, owed to his demonic father and repaid when the enchantress sealed him up: the most famous lovers' night of enchantment, and a disastrous one. Others take the Demon as Vivien herself. Either way the comparison is ominous, since it casts the coming night as a magical entrapment. Keats knew Malory and the story from Spenser (Faerie Queene III.iii).

title: The stained-glass casement
short: A celebrated set piece of stained glass, carved fruits and heraldry, whose richness of sound and colour is often cited as Keats at his most sensuous.
body: The window is described in a crescendo of sound and colour: carved 'imag'ries' of fruits and knot-grass, 'diamonded' panes, 'stains and splendid dyes' compared to a tiger-moth's 'deep-damask'd wings', and at the centre a 'shielded scutcheon' (coat of arms) that 'blush'd with blood of queens and kings', a heraldic way of saying it bore red. The stanza is a standard exhibit of Keats's richly layered sound and colour. The window is both decoration and theological symbol: earthly light becomes coloured, and the next stanza shows it falling on Madeline at prayer.

title: gules on Madeline's breast
short: 'Gules' is heraldic red: the moonlight through the stained glass throws red, rose and amethyst on Madeline, so that she seems haloed like a saint.
body: 'Gules' is heraldry's word for red. The 'wintry moon' shining through the window paints Madeline with colour: red on her breast, 'Rose-bloom' on her hands, amethyst on her cross, and a 'glory' (halo) on her hair. She seems 'a splendid angel, newly drest, / Save wings'. Critics have long noted the optical objection that moonlight is too faint to cast such colours; most reply that the scene is visionary, and the 'warm' red light from a cold moon is the poem's central paradox. Religious and erotic looking fuse here, since this is what Porphyro sees from his hiding place, and he 'grew faint'.

title: mermaid in sea-weed
short: As her dress slips to her knees, Madeline is half-hidden in its folds like a mermaid among weed: an image of beauty that is half-human and half-enchanted.
body: Madeline undresses in stages, freeing her hair, unclasping her 'warmed jewels', loosening her bodice. The mermaid simile keeps the scene within romance and fantasy while making it more sensual. Mermaids are traditionally seductive and dangerous, so the image hints at the ambiguity of who is enchanting whom. She 'dares not look behind', obeying the rite of stanza 6, and so does not see Porphyro.

title: missal among swart Paynims
short: Sleeping Madeline is shut up like a Christian prayer-book kept clasped in a land of dark-skinned pagans: the sense of the simile is disputed.
body: A missal is the book of the Mass; 'Paynims' (Old French paienime) are pagans, especially Muslims in romance; 'swart' means dark. The usual reading is that Madeline, closed in sleep, is like a Christian missal kept clasped shut, and so protected, in a pagan country where no one would open it. Others suggest the missal is used by converted pagans, or that the pagans are Christians in a heathen land. The two readings carry different weight: either Madeline is a sacred object guarded from profane eyes, or she is a sacred object misused. With the alexandrine that follows, the stanza withdraws her from the world before Porphyro's approach.

anchor: As though a rose should shut
title: The rose that becomes a bud
short: An impossible reversal of nature: in sleep Madeline returns to a closed, virginal state, as if a rose could fold back into a bud.
body: The alexandrine closes the stanza with a figure of time running backwards. It recalls the 'full-blown rose' of Porphyro's thought (st. 16), so the lovers are matched as bud and bloom. The image is a high point of the poem's interest in states between waking and sleep ('wakeful swoon', 'Blissfully haven'd both from joy and pain'). Because nature cannot run back, readers see in the line a hint of what will be lost when the dream is entered.

title: The banquet of delicacies
short: Porphyro heaps exotic foods by the bed: a stanza famous for its luscious sounds, and a pointed contrast with Madeline's ritual fast.
body: The catalogue (candied fruits, jellies 'soother than the creamy curd', 'lucent syrops, tinct with cinnamon', manna and dates) is a showpiece of Keatsian synaesthesia, and its sounds are meant to be tasted. 'Manna' recalls the bread from heaven of Exodus 16; 'argosy' is a large merchant ship; Fez (Morocco), Samarcand (Samarkand, on the Silk Road) and Lebanon (its cedars) mark the outer reaches of the romance world. The food is never eaten. Critics read it as a love-offering, a pagan feast, or a seducer's bait set beside a girl who has gone 'supperless to bed'.

title: Morphean amulet
short: Porphyro wishes for a sleep-charm of Morpheus, god of dreams, to keep the revellers' noise from waking Madeline.
body: Morpheus, in Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 11), is the son of Sleep who takes human shapes (morphai) in dreams. An amulet is a charm worn against harm. As the hall door opens, the 'clarion' and 'kettle-drum' briefly break in: Porphyro's anxious aside shows that the dream-world of the chamber is fragile and surrounded by noise. The name also connects with Porphyro's role, since he will 'melt' into Madeline's dream.

title: eremite
short: An eremite is a hermit; Porphyro casts himself as a religious recluse whose heaven is Madeline, mixing devotion and desire.
body: 'Eremite' (Greek eremos, desert) is the older form of 'hermit'. Porphyro's speech, 'Thou art my heaven, and I thine eremite', is the poem's most open use of the religion of love, and he later calls her a 'silver shrine' and himself a 'famish'd pilgrim' (st. 38). The sacred-profane wordplay goes back to Petrarch and to Romeo's pilgrim sonnet in Romeo and Juliet 1.5. Keats used the word again in the sonnet 'Bright star', where the star is a 'sleepless Eremite'.

title: "La belle dame sans mercy"
short: The 'ancient ditty' Porphyro plays is named after Alain Chartier's 1424 poem; Keats would take the title for his own ballad in April 1819.
body: Alain Chartier's La Belle Dame sans Mercy (1424), a dialogue in which a lady refuses a lover who dies of grief, was known in England through an English version printed among Chaucer's works. Keats imagines it as a Provencal troubadour song. The choice is ironic: Madeline is not merciless, and Porphyro is no languishing lover. Three months later Keats wrote his own 'La Belle Dame sans Merci', where a knight is enchanted and abandoned by a faery woman, which reverses the power relation of this scene.

title: "Solution sweet": the consummation
short: Porphyro 'melted' into Madeline's dream: the chemical metaphor (dissolving, blending of scents) is Keats's veiled statement that the lovers make love.
body: 'Solution' is a chemical term (Keats had trained in medicine at Guy's Hospital) for one substance dissolving into another; the rose blends its odour with the violet. In September 1819 Keats revised the stanza to make the consummation more explicit. His friend and the publishers' adviser Richard Woodhouse wrote to the publisher John Taylor that the revision left nothing improper in the wording but made the sense depend on implication, so that the poem became unfit for women readers; Keats is reported to have replied that he did not want ladies to read his poetry. The 1820 text kept the more veiled version. The line is at the centre of the critical debate: Wasserman took it as spiritual fusion, Stillinger as seduction of a half-waking girl.

title: flaw-blown
short: A 'flaw' is a sudden squall of wind: the storm outside returns at the moment the dream gives way to reality.
body: 'Flaw' in this sense (a gust or brief storm) is old and nautical; Shakespeare uses it in Hamlet 5.1 ('to expel the winter's flaw'). The repetition 'Tis dark' and the 'iced gusts' mark the shift from the warm interior of dream to the cold of fact. St Agnes' moon has set: the magic has run out. Porphyro's 'This is no dream, my bride' and Madeline's answering 'No dream, alas!' replace dream with waking fact.

title: "A dove forlorn and lost"
short: Madeline sees herself as a sick dove with 'unpruned' (unpreened) wings: the poem's starkest moment of betrayal.
body: 'Prune' here is the old variant of 'preen', the bird's grooming of its feathers; an unpruned wing is ragged and disordered. Madeline, now fully awake, calls herself 'a deceived thing' and Porphyro a 'traitor'. Her lament supports Stillinger's sceptical reading. Porphyro's reply turns to the language of feudal service and pilgrimage ('vassal', 'famish'd pilgrim', 'saved by miracle') and promises marriage and a home 'o'er the southern moors'. Whether this answers her fear or covers it is left to the reader.

title: The ending: "ages long ago"
short: The final stanza suddenly pushes the story into the far past and ends with nightmare, palsy and death, not the lovers' happiness.
body: The lovers escape past the drunken Porter and the bloodhound, and the poem withdraws: 'ay, ages long ago / These lovers fled away into the storm'. Their fate is unknown. The Baron's guests are 'be-nightmar'd' by witch, demon and 'large coffin-worm'; Angela dies 'palsy-twitch'd'; the Beadsman sleeps 'among his ashes cold'. Readers disagree whether the ending is a fairy-tale escape, an ironic frame showing that romance cannot survive time, or a deliberate refusal of a sentimental close. The return of the Beadsman ties the last line to the first stanza's cold.
